sentences.text: In the HTTP Caching spec, there are two main types of caches: private caches and shared caches.
sentences.subject: caches

sentences.text: A private cache is a cache tied to a specific client — typically a browser cache.
sentences.subject: private cache

sentences.text: Since the stored response is not shared with other clients, a private cache can store a personalized response for that user.
sentences.subject: private cache

sentences.text: On the other hand, if personalized contents are stored in a cache other than a private cache, then other users may be able to retrieve those contents — which may cause unintentional information leakage.
sentences.subject: private cache

sentences.text: If a response contains personalized content and you want to store the response only in the private cache, you must specify a private directive.
sentences.subject: private cache

sentences.text: Personalized contents are usually controlled by cookies, but the presence of a cookie does not always indicate that it is private, and thus a cookie alone does not make the response private.
sentences.subject: private cache

sentences.text: The shared cache is located between the client and the server and can store responses that can be shared among users.
sentences.subject: shared cache

sentences.text: And shared caches can be further sub-classified into proxy caches and managed caches.
sentences.subject: shared cache

sentences.text: In addition to the function of access control, some proxies implement caching to reduce traffic out of the network.
sentences.subject: proxy caches

sentences.text: However, in recent years, as HTTPS has become more common and client/server communication has become encrypted, proxy caches in the path can only tunnel a response and can't behave as a cache, in many cases.
sentences.subject: proxy caches

sentences.text: Managed caches are explicitly deployed by service developers to offload the origin server and to deliver content efficiently.
sentences.subject: managed caches

sentences.text: Examples include reverse proxies, CDNs, and service workers in combination with the Cache API.
sentences.subject: managed caches

sentences.text: In most cases, you can control the cache's behavior through the Cache-Control header and your own configuration files or dashboards.
sentences.subject: managed caches

sentences.text: For example, the HTTP Caching specification essentially does not define a way to explicitly delete a cache — but with a managed cache, the stored response can be deleted at any time through dashboard operations, API calls, restarts, and so on.
sentences.subject: managed caches

sentences.text: That allows for a more proactive caching strategy.
sentences.subject: managed caches

sentences.text: That means if a managed cache intentionally ignores a no-store directive, there is no need to perceive it as being "non-compliant" with the standard.
sentences.subject: managed caches

sentences.text: What you should do is, avoid using kitchen-sink headers, but carefully read the documentation of whatever managed-cache mechanism you're using, and ensure you're controlling the cache properly in the ways provided by the mechanism you've chosen to use.
sentences.subject: managed caches

sentences.text: HTTP is designed to cache as much as possible, so even if no Cache-Control is given, responses will get stored and reused if certain conditions are met.
sentences.subject: heuristic caching

sentences.text: This is called heuristic caching.
sentences.subject: heuristic caching

sentences.text: It is heuristically known that content which has not been updated for a full year will not be updated for some time after that.
sentences.subject: heuristic caching

sentences.text: Therefore, the client stores this response (despite the lack of max-age) and reuses it for a while.
sentences.subject: heuristic caching

sentences.text: How long to reuse is up to the implementation, but the specification recommends about 10% (in this case 0.1 year) of the time after storing.
sentences.subject: heuristic caching

sentences.text: Heuristic caching is a workaround that came before Cache-Control support became widely adopted, and basically all responses should explicitly specify a Cache-Control header.
sentences.subject: heuristic caching

sentences.text: Stored HTTP responses have two states: fresh and stale.
sentences.subject: freshness

sentences.text: The fresh state usually indicates that the response is still valid and can be reused, while the stale state means that the cached response has already expired.
sentences.subject: freshness

sentences.text: The criterion for determining when a response is fresh and when it is stale is age.
sentences.subject: freshness

sentences.text: In HTTP, age is the time elapsed since the response was generated.
sentences.subject: freshness

sentences.text: The cache that stored the example response calculates the time elapsed since the response was generated and uses the result as the response's age.
sentences.subject: freshness

sentences.text: If the age of the response is less than one week, the response is fresh.
sentences.subject: freshness

sentences.text: If the age of the response is more than one week, the response is stale.
sentences.subject: freshness

sentences.text: As long as the stored response remains fresh, it will be used to fulfill client requests.
sentences.subject: freshness

sentences.text: The client which receives that response will find it to be fresh for the remaining 518400 seconds, the difference between the response's max-age and Age.
sentences.subject: freshness

sentences.text: In HTTP/1.0, freshness used to be specified by the Expires header.
sentences.subject: Expires

sentences.text: However, the time format is difficult to parse, many implementation bugs were found, and it is possible to induce problems by intentionally shifting the system clock; therefore, max-age — for specifying an elapsed time — was adopted for Cache-Control in HTTP/1.1.
sentences.subject: Expires

sentences.text: If both Expires and Cache-Control: max-age are available, max-age is defined to be preferred.
sentences.subject: Expires

sentences.text: But the contents of responses are not always the same, even if they have the same URL.
sentences.subject: Vary

sentences.text: Especially when content negotiation is performed, the response from the server can depend on the values of the Accept, Accept-Language, and Accept-Encoding request headers.
sentences.subject: Vary

sentences.text: In this case, you can cause the responses to be cached separately — based on language — by adding Accept-Language to the value of the Vary header.
sentences.subject: Vary

sentences.text: That causes the cache to be keyed based on a composite of the response URL and the Accept-Language request header — rather than being based just on the response URL.
sentences.subject: Vary

sentences.text: However, the User-Agent request header generally has a very large number of variations, which drastically reduces the chance that the cache will be reused.
sentences.subject: Vary

sentences.text: So if possible, instead consider a way to vary behavior based on feature detection rather than based on the User-Agent request header.
sentences.subject: Vary

sentences.text: For applications that employ cookies to prevent others from reusing cached personalized content, you should specify Cache-Control: private instead of specifying a cookie for Vary.
sentences.subject: Vary

sentences.text: Stale responses are not immediately discarded.
sentences.subject: validation

sentences.text: HTTP has a mechanism to transform a stale response into a fresh one by asking the origin server.
sentences.subject: validation

sentences.text: This is called validation, or sometimes, revalidation.
sentences.subject: validation

sentences.text: Validation is done by using a conditional request that includes an If-Modified-Since or If-None-Match request header.
sentences.subject: validation

sentences.text: The server will respond with 304 Not Modified if the content has not changed since the specified time.
sentences.subject: If-Modified-Since

sentences.text: Since this response only indicates "no change", there is no response body — there's just a status code — so the transfer size is extremely small.
sentences.subject: If-Modified-Since

sentences.text: Upon receiving that response, the client reverts the stored stale response back to being fresh and can reuse it during the remaining 1 hour.
sentences.subject: If-Modified-Since

sentences.text: The server can obtain the modification time from the operating-system file system, which is relatively easy to do for the case of serving static files.
sentences.subject: If-Modified-Since

sentences.text: However, there are some problems; for example, the time format is complex and difficult to parse, and distributed servers have difficulty synchronizing file-update times.
sentences.subject: If-Modified-Since

sentences.text: To solve such problems, the ETag response header was standardized as an alternative.
sentences.subject: ETag

sentences.text: The value of the ETag response header is an arbitrary value generated by the server.
sentences.subject: ETag

sentences.text: There are no restrictions on how the server must generate the value, so servers are free to set the value based on whatever means they choose — such as a hash of the body contents or a version number.
sentences.subject: ETag

sentences.text: If that response is stale, the client takes the value of the ETag response header for the cached response, and puts it into the If-None-Match request header, to ask the server if the resource has been modified:
sentences.subject: ETag

sentences.text: The server will return 304 Not Modified if the value of the ETag header it determines for the requested resource is the same as the If-None-Match value in the request.
sentences.subject: ETag

sentences.text: But if the server determines the requested resource should now have a different ETag value, the server will instead respond with a 200 OK and the latest version of the resource.
sentences.subject: ETag

sentences.text: Note: RFC9110 prefers that servers send both ETag and Last-Modified for a 200 response if possible.
sentences.subject: ETag

sentences.text: During cache revalidation, if both If-Modified-Since and If-None-Match are present, then If-None-Match takes precedence for the validator.
sentences.subject: ETag

sentences.text: However, Last-Modified is not just useful for caching; it is a standard HTTP header that is also used by content-management (CMS) systems to display the last-modified time, by crawlers to adjust crawl frequency, and for other various purposes.
sentences.subject: ETag

sentences.text: So considering the overall HTTP ecosystem, it is better to provide both ETag and Last-Modified.
sentences.subject: ETag

sentences.text: If you do not want a response to be reused, but instead want to always fetch the latest content from the server, you can use the no-cache directive to force validation.
sentences.subject: no-cache

sentences.text: By adding Cache-Control: no-cache to the response along with Last-Modified and ETag — as shown below — the client will receive a 200 OK response if the requested resource has been updated, or will otherwise receive a 304 Not Modified response if the requested resource has not been updated.
sentences.subject: no-cache

sentences.text: Note: The no-cache directive (or equivalent, such as max-age=0, must-revalidate) does not guarantee revalidation for history navigations — such as those made using the Back button.
sentences.subject: no-cache

sentences.text: max-age=0 means that the response is immediately stale, and must-revalidate means that it must not be reused without revalidation once it is stale — so, in combination, the semantics seem to be the same as no-cache.
sentences.subject: no-cache

sentences.text: However, that usage of max-age=0 is a remnant of the fact that many implementations prior to HTTP/1.1 were unable to handle the no-cache directive — and so to deal with that limitation, max-age=0 was used as a workaround.
sentences.subject: no-cache

sentences.text: But now that HTTP/1.1-conformant servers are widely deployed, there's no reason to ever use that max-age=0 and must-revalidate combination — you should instead just use no-cache.
sentences.subject: no-cache

sentences.text: The no-cache directive does not prevent the storing of responses but instead prevents the reuse of responses without revalidation.
sentences.subject: no-cache

sentences.text: If you don't want a response stored in any cache, use no-store.
sentences.subject: no-store

sentences.text: Under that set of circumstances, no-store is not always the most-appropriate directive.
sentences.subject: no-store

sentences.text: It would be problematic if a response with personalized content is unexpectedly visible to other users of a cache.
sentences.subject: private

sentences.text: In such a case, using the private directive will cause the personalized response to only be stored with the specific client and not be leaked to any other user of the cache.
sentences.subject: private

sentences.text: The no-store directive prevents a response from being stored, but does not delete any already-stored response for the same URL.
sentences.subject: no-store

sentences.text: In other words, if there is an old response already stored for a particular URL, returning no-store will not prevent the old response from being reused.
sentences.subject: no-store

sentences.text: However, a no-cache directive will force the client to send a validation request before reusing any stored response.
sentences.subject: no-cache

sentences.text: If the server does not support conditional requests, you can force the client to access the server every time and always get the latest response with 200 OK.
sentences.subject: no-cache

sentences.text: It is recommended to use no-cache as an alternative for dealing with such outdated implementations, and it is not a problem if no-cache is given from the beginning, since the server will always receive the request.
sentences.subject: no-cache

sentences.text: If it is the shared cache that you are concerned about, you can make sure to prevent unintended caching by also adding private:
sentences.subject: private

sentences.text: However, it's not recommended to grant no-store liberally, because you lose many advantages that HTTP and browsers have, including the browser's back/forward cache.
sentences.subject: no-store

sentences.text: Therefore, to get the advantages of the full feature set of the web platform, prefer the use of no-cache in combination with private.
sentences.subject: no-cache

sentences.text: Validation can be performed for requests as well as responses.
sentences.subject: reload

sentences.text: The reload and force reload actions are common examples of validation performed from the browser side.
sentences.subject: reload

sentences.text: The max-age=0 directive in the request specifies "reuse of responses with an age of 0 or less" — so, in effect, intermediately stored responses are not reused.
sentences.subject: reload

sentences.text: As a result, a request is validated by If-None-Match and If-Modified-Since.
sentences.subject: reload

sentences.text: Browsers use max-age=0 during reloads for backward-compatibility reasons — because many outdated implementations prior to HTTP/1.1 did not understand no-cache.
sentences.subject: reload

sentences.text: But no-cache is fine now in this use case, and force reload is an additional way to bypass cached responses.
sentences.subject: reload

sentences.text: Since that's not a conditional request with no-cache, you can be sure you'll get a 200 OK from the origin server.
sentences.subject: reload

sentences.text: Content that never changes should be given a long max-age by using cache busting — that is, by including a version number, hash value, etc., in the request URL.
sentences.subject: avoiding revalidation

sentences.text: However, when the user reloads, a revalidation request is sent even though the server knows that the content is immutable.
sentences.subject: avoiding revalidation

sentences.text: To prevent that, the immutable directive can be used to explicitly indicate that revalidation is not required because the content never changes.
sentences.subject: avoiding revalidation

sentences.text: There is no way to delete responses on an intermediate server that have been stored with a long max-age.
sentences.subject: deleting stored responses

sentences.text: You may want to overwrite that response once it expired on the server, but there is nothing the server can do once the response is stored — since no more requests reach the server due to caching.
sentences.subject: deleting stored responses

sentences.text: The Clear-Site-Data: cache header and directive value can be used to clear browser caches — but has no effect on intermediate caches.
sentences.subject: deleting stored responses

sentences.text: Otherwise responses will remain in the browser cache until max-age expires, unless the user manually performs a reload, force-reload, or clear-history action.
sentences.subject: deleting stored responses

sentences.text: Caching reduces access to the server, which means that the server loses control of that URL.
sentences.subject: deleting stored responses

sentences.text: If the server does not want to lose control of a URL — for example, in the case that a resource is frequently updated — you should add no-cache so that the server will always receive requests and send the intended responses.
sentences.subject: deleting stored responses

sentences.text: The shared cache is primarily located before the origin server and is intended to reduce traffic to the origin server.
sentences.subject: request collapse

sentences.text: Thus, if multiple identical requests arrive at a shared cache at the same time, the intermediate cache will forward a single request on behalf of itself to the origin, which can then reuse the result for all clients.
sentences.subject: request collapse

sentences.text: This is called request collapse.
sentences.subject: request collapse

sentences.text: Request collapse occurs when requests are arriving at the same time, so even if max-age=0 or no-cache is given in the response, it will be reused.
sentences.subject: request collapse

sentences.text: If the response is personalized to a particular user and you do not want it to be shared in collapse, you should add the private directive:
sentences.subject: request collapse

sentences.text: But most websites can be covered by a combination of a handful of patterns.
sentences.subject: common caching patterns

sentences.text: As mentioned above, the default behavior for caching (that is, for a response without Cache-Control) is not simply "don't cache" but implicit caching according to so-called "heuristic caching".
sentences.subject: default settings

sentences.text: To avoid that heuristic caching, it's preferable to explicitly give all responses a default Cache-Control header.
sentences.subject: default settings

sentences.text: To ensure that by default the latest versions of resources will always be transferred, it's common practice to make the default Cache-Control value include no-cache:
sentences.subject: default settings

sentences.text: In addition, if the service implements cookies or other login methods, and the content is personalized for each user, private must be given too, to prevent sharing with other users:
sentences.subject: default settings

sentences.text: The resources that work best with caching are static immutable files whose contents never change.
sentences.subject: cache busting

sentences.text: And for resources that do change, it is a common best practice to change the URL each time the content changes, so that the URL unit can be cached for a longer period.
sentences.subject: cache busting

sentences.text: So the HTML above makes it difficult to cache bundle.js and build.css with max-age.
sentences.subject: cache busting

sentences.text: Therefore, you can serve the JavaScript and CSS with URLs that include a changing part based on a version number or hash value.
sentences.subject: cache busting

sentences.text: Since the cache distinguishes resources from one another based on their URLs, the cache will not be reused again if the URL changes when a resource is updated.
sentences.subject: cache busting

sentences.text: With that design, both JavaScript and CSS resources can be cached for a long time.
sentences.subject: cache busting

sentences.text: Because the cache removes old entries when new entries are saved, the probability that a stored response still exists after one week is not that high — even if max-age is set to 1 week.
sentences.subject: QPACK

sentences.text: Therefore, in practice, it does not make much difference which one you choose.
sentences.subject: QPACK

sentences.text: The public value has the effect of making the response storable even if the Authorization header is present.
sentences.subject: public

sentences.text: Note: The public directive should only be used if there is a need to store the response when the Authorization header is set.
sentences.subject: public

sentences.text: So if the response is personalized with basic authentication, the presence of public may cause problems.
sentences.subject: public

sentences.text: Don't forget to set the Last-Modified and ETag headers, so that you don't have to re-transmit a resource when reloading.
sentences.subject: validation

sentences.text: In addition, immutable can be added to prevent validation on reload.
sentences.subject: avoiding revalidation

sentences.text: Cache busting is a technique to make a response cacheable over a long period by changing the URL when the content changes.
sentences.subject: cache busting

sentences.text: The technique can be applied to all subresources, such as images.
sentences.subject: cache busting

sentences.text: Unlike subresources, main resources cannot be cache busted because their URLs can't be decorated in the same way that subresource URLs can be.
sentences.subject: main resources

sentences.text: If the following HTML itself is stored, the latest version cannot be displayed even if the content is updated on the server side.
sentences.subject: main resources

sentences.text: For that case, no-cache would be appropriate — rather than no-store — since we don't want to store HTML, but instead just want it to always be up-to-date.
sentences.subject: main resources

sentences.text: Furthermore, adding Last-Modified and ETag will allow clients to send conditional requests, and a 304 Not Modified can be returned if there have been no updates to the HTML:
sentences.subject: main resources

sentences.text: That setting is appropriate for non-personalized HTML, but for a response that gets personalized using cookies — for example, after a login — don't forget to also specify private:
sentences.subject: main resources

sentences.text: The same can be used for favicon.ico, manifest.json, .well-known, and API endpoints whose URLs cannot be changed using cache busting.
sentences.subject: main resources

sentences.text: Most web content can be covered by a combination of the two patterns described above.
sentences.subject: common caching patterns

sentences.text: With the method described in previous sections, subresources can be cached for a long time by using cache busting, but main resources (which are usually HTML documents) can't be.
sentences.subject: cache busting

sentences.text: Caching main resources is difficult because, using just standard directives from the HTTP Caching specification, there's no way to actively delete cache contents when content is updated on the server.
sentences.subject: main resources

sentences.text: However, it is possible by deploying a managed cache such as a CDN or service worker.
sentences.subject: main resources

sentences.text: For example, a CDN that allows cache purging via an API or dashboard operation would allow for a more aggressive caching strategy by storing the main resource and explicitly purging the relevant cache only when an update occurs on the server.
sentences.subject: main resources
